_comment: How Levantine Arabic (the urban speech of Damascus, Beirut and Jerusalem) says the letters a romanisation of standard Arabic writes, for lib/translit.py: read before lib/lang/ar.ipa.json for a book or a video written in Levantine (variety ar.lev). Whatever this file does not say is ar.ipa.json's. ONLY the consonant correspondences every description of urban Levantine gives; the case endings go (`from_standard.pausal`, the rule in ar.ipa.json: kataba > katab, kitābun > kitāb); the vowels and stress are not touched.
_sources: Mark W. Cowell, A Reference Grammar of Syrian Arabic (Georgetown University Press, 1964), ch. 1: Damascene q > ʔ and the interdentals > stops in the inherited words.
Janet C. E. Watson, The Phonology and Morphology of Arabic (Oxford University Press, 2002), ch. 2.
Kees Versteegh, The Arabic Language, 2nd ed. (Edinburgh University Press, 2014), ch. 10 (the Syro-Lebanese dialects).

from_standard._map: A letter of the standard romanisation (the standard dictionary's hits, shown in a text written in Levantine) to the letter the cities say. ق is a glottal stop (qalb > ʾalb); ث ذ ظ are t d ḍ in the inherited words (ṯalāṯa > talāta, ḏahab > dahab, ẓahr > ḍahr). ج is LEFT j: it is ž in Damascus and Beirut and j further south, and the Levantine dictionary itself writes j (304 of its 325 entries with ج), so one sound keeps one letter in the panel. Left to the research brief with it: ق as g or k in the countryside, and the words from the written language that keep q, s, z, ẓ.

roman._keep_initial: The Levantine dictionary writes a word that begins with ق with its glottal stop (قلب ʔalb): that ʾ is the word's first consonant and is kept, where the hamza of a word that begins with a vowel is dropped as ar.ipa.json says.
